# How to read this document

This document is divided into sections based on specific topics. In each section there is a set of summary main bullet points, a description of the analysis done in that section to support those bullet points, and the output from the analysis done in that section. The main bullet points cover a combination of answering the questions in the empirical paper and the overall questions about how each of the estimators perform under different conditions. The analysis descriptions need to be moved to be under the piece of analysis they describe, but for now I thought it was better to have it all up top. 

\newpage

# What does the bias look like for each estimator 


## Main Bullet Points:

- The estimators theory says are unbiased do indeed have no bias (or have very low bias) across the full range of simulations

- For most of the estimators that are biased, the mean bias is mostly driven by large differences across blocks. With the largest bias in cases with large differences across blocks, 10 or 20 clusters, and unbalanced assignment to treatment (mean p =.7).

- The LRapw−FIpw−db has bias as large as -.033, which from the regression tree is an driven by a correlation between the treatment effect and cluster size and then variance in cluster size and treatment effect. This is consistent with theory.  

## Description of Analysis

- The first graph is a boxplot of mean bias across the different scenarios by method. The faint horizontal lines go out to the full range, the bars are the 1% to 99%, and the boxes are the 10% to 90%.

- The second graph is a regression tree which predicts the magnitude of the mean bias using different data generating parameters and also flags for if the method is an MLM, is fully interacted, is cluster weighted, or is person weighted.

- The third graph is a the same regression tree above, but just for the LRapw−FIpw−db. The indicators for MLM, FI, cluster weighted, and person weighted are dropped for this regression.   

- The first table contains the DGPs that produce that largest magnitude of mean bias for each method, conditional on the magnitude of the mean bias being at least .1 . Where again mean bias is the mean bias against the targeted estimator.

```{r biasmodel, include=FALSE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

# Create a list to store models
models_by_method <- list()
model_summaries <- list()

# Run separate models for each method
for (m in core.methods) {
  # Subset data for this method
  method_data <- sruns.clean %>% filter(method == m)
  
  # Run the model for this method
  # Note: I'm using bias.s.estimand as you specified in your formula
  # Make sure this column exists or replace with the correct one
  models_by_method[[m]] <- lm(bias.s.estimand.mag ~ (block_type + J.bar + size.impact.cor.school + 
                                                 sd.school + ICC.school + 
                                                 cv.school + num.cov.school)^2, 
                              data = method_data)
  
  # Store summary statistics
  model_summaries[[m]] <- broom::tidy(models_by_method[[m]])
  
}


# Helper function to add significance stars
  add_stars <- function(p_value) {
    if (is.na(p_value)) return("")
    if (p_value < 0.001) return("***")
    if (p_value < 0.01) return("**") 
    if (p_value < 0.05) return("*")
    if (p_value < 0.1) return(".")
    return("")
  }


# Function to create a coefficient table with wrapped term names
create_coefficient_table <- function(model_list) {
  # Get all unique terms across all models
  all_terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(model_list, function(m) {
    coef_names <- names(coef(m))
    return(coef_names)
  })))
  
  # Create extraction functions
  extract_coef <- function(model, term) {
    if(term %in% names(coef(model))) {
      return(coef(model)[term])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }
  
  extract_p <- function(model, term) {
    if(term %in% rownames(summary(model)$coefficients)) {
      return(summary(model)$coefficients[term, "Pr(>|t|)"])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }
  
  # Function to wrap long term names
  wrap_term <- function(term, width = 25) {
    if (nchar(term) <= width) {
      return(term)
    }
    
    # For interaction terms (with :), try to break at the colon
    if (grepl(":", term)) {
      # Replace ":" with newline character
      wrapped <- gsub(":", ":\n", term)
      return(wrapped)
    }
    
    # Otherwise, use general text wrapping logic
    # Find a good breaking point
    break_point <- width
    while (break_point > 0 && substr(term, break_point, break_point) != " " && 
           substr(term, break_point, break_point) != "_") {
      break_point <- break_point - 1
    }
    
    if (break_point == 0) {
      # If no good breaking point, just break at width
      break_point <- width
    }
    
    # Insert newline character
    wrapped <- paste0(
      substr(term, 1, break_point),
      "\n",
      substr(term, break_point + 1, nchar(term))
    )
    
    return(wrapped)
  }
  
  # Create result dataframe
  result <- data.frame(Term = sapply(all_terms, wrap_term), 
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  # Add coefficients for each method with shorter formatting

  for(m in names(model_list)) {

    coefs <- sapply(all_terms, function(t) extract_coef(model_list[[m]], t))
    p_vals <- sapply(all_terms, function(t) extract_p(model_list[[m]], t))
    stars <- sapply(p_vals, add_stars)
coef_strings <- ifelse(
  !is.na(coefs),
  ifelse(
    round(coefs,3) == 0,
    paste0("<.001", stars),  # Just "0" for zero values
    paste0(
      # Drop leading zero for values between -1 and 1
      sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", sprintf("%.3f", coefs)),
      stars
    )
  ),
  "")
    
    
    # Use abbreviated method names if they're too long
   method_name <- ifelse(nchar(m) > 15, 
                          paste0(substr(m, 1, 14), "."), 
                        m)
    
    # Add to result
    result[[method_name]] <- coef_strings
  }
  
  return(result)
}

# Generate the coefficient table
coef_table <- create_coefficient_table(models_by_method)

# Set row names to NULL
row.names(coef_table) <- NULL

# Set pander options
panderOptions('table.split.table', Inf)  # Allow table to split across pages
panderOptions('table.style', 'multiline')  # More compact style
panderOptions('p.wrap', TRUE)  # Enable text wrapping - CHANGED FROM FALSE TO TRUE
panderOptions('keep.trailing.zeros', FALSE)
panderOptions('digits', 3)

# Create header for the table
cat("\n")
cat("### The Effect of Different Data Generating Parameters on the Magnitude of Mean Bias \n\n")

# Create a custom alignment vector - LEFT justify the first column, RIGHT justify all others
justify <- c('left', rep('center', ncol(coef_table)-1))

# For PDF output - wrap pander table in font size commands
cat("\\begingroup\n")
cat("\\footnotesize\n")  # This will make the font smaller

pander(coef_table, 
       justify = justify,
       style = 'multiline',
       split.tables = Inf)
# Add significance note
cat("\n*Significance: '\\*\\*\\*' 0.001 '\\*\\*' 0.01 '\\*' 0.05 '.' 0.1*\n")
cat("\\endgroup\n")  # This restores the previous font size


# Add a footnote explaining significance levels
add_significance_footnote <- function(table_object) {
  footnote(table_object,
    general = "Significance codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1",
    general_title = "Note: "
  )
}

# Create comparison table with significance stars - MODIFIED to make narrower output
create_star_comparison_table <- function(model_list) {
  # Initialize a list to store tidy model outputs
  tidy_models <- list()
  
  # Process each model
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    # Get model coefficients and p-values
    model_stats <- tidy(model_list[[m]]) %>%
      # Create a column with coefficient and stars - USING SHORTER FORMAT
      mutate(
        stars = sapply(p.value, add_stars),
        # Reduce number of decimal places from 3 to 2 to save space
        coef_stars = ifelse(!is.na(estimate),
                            sprintf("%.2f%s", estimate, stars),
                            "")
      )
    
    # Add to our list
    tidy_models[[m]] <- model_stats
  }
  
  # Combine all models into a single data frame
  all_terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(tidy_models, function(x) x$term)))
  
  # Initialize result dataframe
  result <- data.frame(term = all_terms)
  
  # Add each method's coefficients as a column
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    temp_df <- tidy_models[[m]] %>% 
      select(term, coef_stars)
    
    # Rename to method name - USING SHORTER METHOD NAMES if needed
    # If method names are long, you could abbreviate them here
    # For example: names(temp_df)[2] <- substr(m, 1, 3)  # First 3 chars only
    names(temp_df)[2] <- m
    
    # Join to result
    result <- result %>% 
      left_join(temp_df, by = "term")
  }
  
  return(result)
}



  
```


# What does the standard error look like for each estimator 

## Main Bullet Points:

- For the person weighted estimators, the unbiased estimator both has less error and is more stable than the biased estimator. 

- For the cluster weighted estimators, the unbiased estimator generally has less error than the biased estimators but more instablity. 

- The MLM estimators are the most stable, which fits with theory. 

- High RMSE and estimate instability is driven by a cluster ICC and a low number of clusters

## Answers to Questions In the Emperical Paper 

- Re the question on pg. 39, looking at the second boxplot shows that true S.E. do vary across estimators with the true standard error in a given DGP often 40% bigger for some estimates than the median estimate in that DPG. 

## Description of Analysis:

- The first graph is a boxplot of the normalized RMSE across the different scenarios by method. The normalized RMSE is the RMSE for given method divided by the median RMSE across methods within a given simulation scenario. Therefore each data point is adjusted for the underlying base RMSE from a given set of DGPs and represents the RMSE driven by the estimation method.

- The second graph is a boxplot of the normalized estimate standard deviation across the different scenarios by method. This is also normalized by dividing by the median estimate standard deviation within a given simulation scenario. 

- The third graph is a regression tree which predicts the root mean squared error (RMSE) against the targeted estimand using different data generating parameters and also flags for if the method is an MLM, is fully interacted, is cluster weighted, or is person weighted.


- The fourth graph is a regression tree which predicts the true super population standard error using different data generating parameters and also flags for if the method is an MLM, is fully interacted, is cluster weighted, or is person weighted.

- The first table contains the five DGPs that produce the five most normalized RMSE (against the targeted estimator) for each method, conditional on the magnitude of the being at least 1.10. 

- The fourth table contains the five DGPs that produce the most normalized super population standard error for each method, conditional on the magnitude of the being at least 1.10.

# What do the estimated standard errors look like for each estimator

## Main Bullet Points:

- This section answers the rest of the questions from pg.39 (i.e. are certain SE estimators more accurate than others) 

- For the cluster targeted estimates the fully interacted estimators produce more accurate standard errors than the other estimators (graph one). The unbiased estimators produce more unstable estimates than the biased estimators, but in 90% of the DGP we looked at they aren't a lot more unstable (graph four).

- For the person targeted estimates the fully interacted estimators produce more accurate standard errors than the other estimators (graphs one, two and three). The fully interacted estimators produce more unstable estimates than the other estimators (graph four). However they aren't a lot more unstable, 90% of the time they're within about 10% of the median instability and fully interacted doesn't come up in the regression tree (graph five). 

- This section also answers the question from pg. 38 about the instability of the estimated standard errors for the fully interacted models. The simulations do not really show that the standard errors from the fully interacted models are lot more unstable than the other standard errors. We should talk about this more, and what would be helpful for me to dig into more. 


## Description of Analysis:

- The first graph is a boxplot of the estimated standard error accuracy across the different scenarios by method. Standard error accuracy is quantified as the estimated standard error over the true super population standard error. Estimated standard errors are most accurate if the number is close to one. Numbers below one represent under estimated standard errors and numbers above one represent over estimated standard errors. [Luke had a comment on this graph that I couldn't read and need to follow up on]

- The second graph is a regression tree which predicts the standard error inflation (estimated standard error over the true super population standard error) using different data generating parameters and also flags for if the method is an MLM, is fully interacted, is cluster weighted, or is person weighted.

-  For the third graph, I was having trouble conceptualizing the scale of standard error inflation, so I made a regression tree where I converted it to percentage inaccuracy. The regression tree here is therefore predicting the magnitude of ((Mean Estimated SE - True Super Population SE) / True Super Population SE) * 100.  

- The first table contains the five DGPs that produce the most inaccurate standard error estimates for each method, conditional on the magnitude of the inaccuracy being at least .1. 

- The fourth graph is a boxplot of the standard deviation of the estimated standard error across the different replications divided by the true estimate standard error by method. 

- The fifth graph is a boxplot of the normalized standard deviation of the estimated standard error across the different replications by method. 

- The sixth graph is a regression tree which predicts instability in the standard error estimate using different data generating parameters and also flags for if the method is an MLM, is fully interacted, is cluster weighted, or is person weighted.  Here  instability in the standard error estimate is quantified as the standard deviation of the estimated standard error across the different replications divided by the true estimate standard error by method

- The second table contains the five DGPs that produce the largest standard deviation in the standard error estimates for each method, conditional on the magnitude being at least .05. 

- The third table contains the five DGPs that produce the largest normalized standard deviation in the standard error estimates for each method, conditional on the magnitude being at least 1.10.

```{r semodel, include=FALSE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
# Function to create a coefficient table with wrapped term names
create_coefficient_table_wide <- function(model_list) {
  # Get all unique terms across all models
  all_terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(model_list, function(m) {
    coef_names <- names(coef(m))
    return(coef_names)
  })))
  
  # Create extraction functions
  extract_coef <- function(model, term) {
    if(term %in% names(coef(model))) {
      return(coef(model)[term])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }
  
  extract_p <- function(model, term) {
    if(term %in% rownames(summary(model)$coefficients)) {
      return(summary(model)$coefficients[term, "Pr(>|t|)"])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }
  
  # Function to wrap long term names
  wrap_term <- function(term, width = 13) {
    if (nchar(term) <= width) {
      return(term)
    }
    
    # For interaction terms (with :), try to break at the colon
    if (grepl(":", term)) {
      # Replace ":" with newline character
      wrapped <- gsub(":", ":\n", term)
      return(wrapped)
    }
    
    # Otherwise, use general text wrapping logic
    # Find a good breaking point
    break_point <- width
    while (break_point > 0 && substr(term, break_point, break_point) != " " && 
           substr(term, break_point, break_point) != "_") {
      break_point <- break_point - 1
    }
    
    if (break_point == 0) {
      # If no good breaking point, just break at width
      break_point <- width
    }
    
    # Insert newline character
    wrapped <- paste0(
      substr(term, 1, break_point),
      "\n",
      substr(term, break_point + 1, nchar(term))
    )
    
    return(wrapped)
  }
  
  # Create result dataframe
  result <- data.frame(Term = sapply(all_terms, wrap_term), 
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  # Add coefficients for each method with shorter formatting

  for(m in names(model_list)) {

    coefs <- sapply(all_terms, function(t) extract_coef(model_list[[m]], t))
    p_vals <- sapply(all_terms, function(t) extract_p(model_list[[m]], t))
    stars <- sapply(p_vals, add_stars)
coef_strings <- ifelse(
  !is.na(coefs),
  ifelse(
    round(coefs,3) == 0,
    paste0("<.001", stars),  # Just "0" for zero values
    paste0(
      # Drop leading zero for values between -1 and 1
      sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", sprintf("%.3f", coefs)),
      stars
    )
  ),
  "")
    
    
    # Use abbreviated method names if they're too long
   method_name <- ifelse(nchar(m) > 15, 
                          paste0(substr(m, 1, 14), "."), 
                        m)
    
    # Add to result
    result[[method_name]] <- coef_strings
  }
  
  return(result)
}
```

# Are the estimated standard errors targeting the finite or super population

## Main Bullet Points:

- This section answers the questions on page 8.

- As long as the school level ICC isn't zero, than the true finite and super population standard errors are very similar to each other (graph 2). 

- I was having a little trouble visualizing whether the standard errors were targeting the finite population or super population standard errors, so I made up this metric: difference in % inaccuracy. This is calculated as the magnitude of ((Mean Estimated SE - True Super Population SE) / True Super Population SE) x 100 minus the magnitude of  ((Mean Estimated SE - True Finite Population SE) / True Finite Population SE) x 100. When this number is positive the estimated standard errors are closer to the true super population standard errors and when this number is negative the estimated standard errors are closer to the finite population. 

- The only estimators with standard errors that are ever really significantly closer to the finite standard errors than the super population standard errors are the person weighted fully interacted ones and the fully interacted MLMs (graphs three and four). It does look like the person weighted fully interacted estimators are targeting the finite standard errors when the ICC is zero, the blocks are very dissimilar, and there is high variance in the cluster sizes. Otherwise these estimators are also targeting super population standard errors (graph five).  


Description of Analysis:

- The first graph is a boxplot of ratio of the true finite standard errors over the true super population standard errors across the different scenarios by method. When this metric is one the two standard errors are the same, when it's above one the finite population standard errors are bigger and when it's below one the super population standard errors are bigger. 

- The second graph is the same as the first but broken out by ICC. In the graph on the left the school level ICC is .20 and on the right it's zero.

- The third graph is a boxplot of the difference in % inaccuracy across methods. This is calculated as the magnitude of ((Mean Estimated SE - True Super Population SE) / True Super Population SE) x 100 minus the magnitude of  ((Mean Estimated SE - True Finite Population SE) / True Finite Population SE) x 100. When this number is positive the estimated standard errors are closer to the true super population standard errors and when this number is negative the estimated standard errors are closer to the finite population. 

- The fourth graph is the same as the third but broken out by ICC. In the graph on the left the school level ICC is .20 and on the right it's zero.

- The fifth graph is a boxplot of the difference in % inaccuracy across methods, but only for the methods that might be targeting the finite population standard errors and only when the school level ICC is zero, the blocks are all messy, and the cluster size coefficient of variation is large. 

- The table contains the five DGPs that produce the largest difference in % inaccuracy for each method, conditional on the magnitude being at least five percentage points.

# What do the confidence intervals look like for each estimator 

## Main Bullet Points

- Coverage is the percentage of simulation replications where the estimator is within the 95% confidence interval. We would like the number to be 95% (the boxplots have a line there). The notable things are that the coverage for the MLM estimators are often very bad but other than that the coverage for the cluster weighted estimators are generally good. The coverage rates for the person weighted estimators however are pretty bad across methods, it's either very low (meaning the SEs are being underestimated) or too high (meaning the SEs are being overestimated within the same methods. 

Description of Analysis:

- The first graph is a boxplot of the coverage by method. Coverage is the percentage of treatment effect estimates that fall in the 95% confidence interval. The vertical line is at 95%, which is what coverage should be.  

- The second graph is a boxplot of the normalized 95% confidence interval length by method.

# Is Low Degrees of Freedom Causing Problems because of Estimate Instability Driven or Bias  

## Main Bullet Points

- This is answering the question on page 35

- Low degrees of freedom is clearly causing problems because of estimate instability. There is clear increase in estimate instability for the low degrees of freedom DGPs (graph one) and no relation between degrees of freedom and mean bias (graph two).  

## Description of Analysis:

- The first graph is scatter plot of the true estimate standard error across replications against the model degrees of freedom, graphed sepparately for each method


- The second graph is scatter plot of the mean bias across replications against the model degrees of freedom, graphed sepparately for each method


```{r degfree, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

ggplot(sruns.graph.bias, aes(x = mean.df, y = SE.s)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = method)) +  # Color is still by method
  facet_wrap(~ method) +  # This creates separate panels for each method
  labs(
    title = "Estimate Instability versus Degrees of Freedom by Model",
    x = "Degrees of Freedom",
    y = "True Estimate Standard Error"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  xlim(c(0, 100)) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgray", color = NA),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid = element_blank()  # This removes all grid lines
  )


ggplot(sruns.graph.bias, aes(x = mean.df, y =  bias.s.estimand)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = method)) +  # Color is still by method
  facet_wrap(~ method) +  # This creates separate panels for each method
  labs(
    title = "Mean Bias versus Degrees of Freedom by Model",
    x = "Degrees of Freedom",
    y = "Mean Bias"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  xlim(c(0, 100)) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightgray", color = NA),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid = element_blank()  # This removes all grid lines
  )
```

```{r old, include=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
{ggplot(plot_data_long, aes(x = method_ordered, y = inflation_value, color = inflation_type)) + 
  # Add reference line at 1.0
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
  
  # Add faint min/max lines in background
  geom_linerange(
    stat = "summary",
    fun.data = function(x) {
      data.frame(ymin = min(x), ymax = max(x))
    },
    alpha = 0.2,
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  
  # Add 1% and 99% whiskers
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = function(x) {
      percentiles <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.01, 0.99))
      return(data.frame(ymin = percentiles[1], ymax = percentiles[2]))
    },
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.5,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
  ) +
  
  # Add custom boxplot for 10% to 90%
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = function(x) {
      r <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9))
      names(r) <- c("ymin", "lower", "middle", "upper", "ymax")
      r
    },
    geom = "boxplot",
    alpha = 0.7,
    width = 0.5,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
  ) +
  
  # Labs and formatting

#This plot is my attempt to show that the SE are mostly targeting super population
{
# Calculate the metrics for each method
comparison_data <- plot_data %>%
  group_by(method_ordered) %>%
  summarize(
    pct_s_closer_to_one = mean(round(abs(inflate.s - 1),2) < round(abs(inflate.f - 1),2)) * 100,
    pct_same = mean(round(abs(inflate.s - 1),2) == round(abs(inflate.f - 1),2)) * 100,
    pct_same_oreq = mean(round(abs(inflate.s - 1),2) <= round(abs(inflate.f - 1),2)) * 100
  ) %>%
  # Convert to long format for plotting
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(pct_s_closer_to_one, pct_same, pct_same_oreq),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "percentage"
  )

# Create nice labels for the metrics
comparison_data$metric <- factor(
  comparison_data$metric,
  levels = c("pct_s_closer_to_one", "pct_same", "pct_same_oreq"),
  labels = c("Estimated SE Closer to Super", "Super = Finite","Estimated SE Closer or Equal to Super")
)}

# Create the bar chart
ggplot(comparison_data, aes(x = method_ordered, y = percentage, fill = metric)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(width = 0.9)) +
  #geom_hline(yintercept = 100, color="black")+
  labs(
    title = "Standard Errors are Mostly Targetting Super Population",
    x = "Method",
    y = "Percentage of Scenarios",
    fill = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  coord_flip()
```
